**CFPB rewrites US open banking rule with data limits and fintech fees**

*The CFPB's revised Section 1033 proposal would cap the data fintechs can access and introduce fees for bank-provided APIs, a material shift from the original rule that European open finance providers with US exposure will need to watch closely.*

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is preparing a revised open banking framework that would allow consumers to share bank data with third parties but impose new restrictions on how much data fintechs can access and permit banks to charge for API connections. The revised rule represents a significant departure from the version finalised under the Biden administration, which had been paused by legal challenges and the CFPB's own internal upheaval.

The changes reflect sustained lobbying by large US banks, which argued the original rule imposed disproportionate costs while letting fintechs access data without adequate compensation. By introducing data minimisation principles and a fee mechanism, the CFPB is moving closer to a model that resembles aspects of PSD3's data-sharing provisions, where access is neither unlimited nor free.

For European open banking providers operating in or eyeing the US market, the revised framework reshapes the commercial dynamics. Firms that built US strategies around broad, free data access will need to recalibrate. The rule also feeds into the broader transatlantic divergence on whether open banking infrastructure should be treated as a utility or a commercial product.

*Sources: [CFPB To Introduce Data Limits And Fees For Fintechs In Revised Open Banking Framework](https://www.crowdfundinsider.com/2026/06/288391-cfpb-to-introduce-data-limits-and-fees-for-fintechs-in-revised-open-banking-framework/) — Crowdfund Insider | [Open banking regulation in 2026: federal regulation resurfaces as states bring data sharing into…](https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/open-banking-regulation-in-2026-federal-7403206/) — JD Supra*

**Crédit Agricole completes France's first production agentic payment**

*Crédit Agricole, Mastercard and Worldline have carried out France's first agentic payment transaction in a production environment, extending the pattern set by ING's Dutch pilot earlier this month into a second major European market.*

The transaction marks the second production-grade agentic payment completed in Europe, following the ING, Worldline and Mastercard pilot in the Netherlands on June 3. That Crédit Agricole — France's largest retail bank by customers — has moved to production rather than sandbox testing suggests the infrastructure for AI-initiated payments is maturing faster than many anticipated.

Agentic payments, where an AI agent initiates and completes a transaction on behalf of a user, have emerged as a theme across the payments industry in recent weeks. Visa's partnership with OpenAI, Santander's Getnet launch and Alipay's token-based system all point in the same direction, but the European implementations are notable for running through established card network and bank infrastructure rather than building parallel systems.

The speed of adoption across different European markets raises practical questions about authentication, liability and consumer consent that existing regulatory frameworks do not yet fully address. The Euro Banking Association's recent mapping exercise on agentic AI in open finance underscores how much of the governance framework remains to be defined.

*Sources: [Crédit Agricole completes agentic payment transaction](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48008/crdit-agricole-completes-agentic-payment-transaction) — Finextra*

**UK banks launch shared digital identity service for app-based KYC**

*The six major UK banks that originally built open banking infrastructure have launched a shared digital identity framework, aiming to replace document-based KYC with reusable, app-based verification.*

The service allows customers to verify their identity once through their banking app and reuse that verified identity across participating institutions, eliminating repeated document uploads. The consortium behind the initiative — the same group of banks that were mandated to build open banking APIs under the CMA order — is positioning the framework as an open standard available to the wider market.

The move extends the institutional architecture created for open banking into adjacent use cases. Reusable digital identity has long been identified as a prerequisite for scaling open finance, since onboarding friction remains one of the primary barriers to adoption. By anchoring the identity layer in existing banking apps that consumers already trust, the consortium sidesteps the adoption challenges that have plagued standalone digital identity schemes in the UK.

The timing aligns with the UK government's recent proposal to use open banking for age verification on social media and the broader Smart Data 2035 strategy. It also comes as the FCA's open finance roadmap places identity verification at the centre of its implementation plan. Whether smaller banks and fintechs can participate on equal terms will determine whether this becomes genuine infrastructure or a competitive moat for the largest institutions.

*Sources: [UK Lenders Launch Open Standard Digital ID Framework to Eliminate KYC Document Friction](https://www.bobsguide.com/uk-lenders-launch-open-standard-digital-id-framework-to-eliminate-kyc-document-friction/) — Bobsguide*

**Banks turn to AI to recover funds after instant payments clear**

*Financial institutions are deploying AI systems to trace and recover stolen funds after instant payment transactions settle, as the irrevocability of real-time rails compounds fraud losses.*

PYMNTS reports that 40% of financial institutions have increased fraud losses linked to instant payments, driven by the fundamental characteristic that makes the rails attractive: finality. Once an instant payment clears, there is no recall mechanism. Banks are now investing in AI tools that can trace fund movements across accounts in real time, identify mule account patterns and trigger freezes at receiving institutions before stolen money is withdrawn or moved again.

The challenge is structural. Europe's SEPA instant payments regulation, which mandates universal availability from October, will dramatically expand the volume of irrevocable transactions flowing through the system. Verification of payee remains incomplete across Europe, a gap this briefing has previously covered. Without pre-transaction checks, the burden shifts to post-transaction recovery, which is inherently less effective.

The UK's experience is instructive. Fraud losses rose to £1.3 billion this year, with APP scams rebounding sharply despite mandatory reimbursement rules. The PSR's data shows reimbursement is working as a consumer protection measure, but it has not reduced the underlying fraud rate. AI-driven fund tracing represents an attempt to address the gap between prevention and recovery, though its effectiveness at scale remains unproven.

*Sources: [Banks Deploy AI to Chase Stolen Funds After Instant Payments Clear](https://www.pymnts.com/news/banking/2026/banks-deploy-ai-to-chase-stolen-funds-after-instant-payments-clear/) — PYMNTS*
